The second experiment (with added product) shifted the ranking, placing deactivation mechanisms (M14, M20, M11) at the top. This suggests that irreversible deactivation of catalyst species is an important feature. However, the NLL values for the top candidates are very close, indicating that more data is needed to distinguish among them. The aim of the second turn was to test product sensitivity, which successfully demoted activation mechanisms (M6, M8) and highlighted deactivation pathways. Now, we need to discriminate within the deactivation cluster, particularly between first-order and second-order deactivation processes.

<hypothesis>
The leading candidates differ in the molecularity of deactivation. M14 (catS -> inactive_catS) and M11 (S+cat -> inactive_catS) are first-order in catalyst-containing species, while M19 (cat+catS -> inactive_cat2S) is second-order. By doubling the catalyst concentration while keeping substrate high, we can test the scaling of deactivation rate relative to initial rate. If deactivation is first-order, the normalized time course (product per catalyst) should resemble that of the first experiment (cat=0.05). If deactivation is second-order, the normalized curve will show a more rapid slowdown because deactivation scales quadratically with catalyst. This experiment also tests other second-order deactivation mechanisms (e.g., M18, M13) and helps separate M9 (simple catalyst decay) from more complex deactivation pathways.
</hypothesis>
